title: Covering Index for a Filtered Aggregate
description: A ranged aggregate scans and hash-aggregates the whole table; a covering index over the range seeks and aggregates a small slice. Why it matters: date-ranged aggregate reports (sales this month, activity this week) are a core business-reporting pattern, and this technique keeps them fast as data accumulates.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Imagine you keep a giant year-by-year ledger of every transaction your business has ever made, and someone asks "what were total sales just this month?" If your ledger has no way to jump straight to this month's entries, you have to flip through every single page of the entire ledger, from day one, checking each entry's date, just to add up a tiny recent slice of it. This lesson is about exactly that situation — a date-ranged summary query that ends up reading far more data than it logically needs to, and how a well-designed index fixes it.

**What this lesson's topic actually is.** This lesson combines two ideas covered elsewhere in this course — range filters (like `WHERE OrderDate >= '2024-01-01'`) and aggregation (`GROUP BY` / `SUM` / `COUNT`) — into one very common real-world shape: "summarize the data, but only for a specific recent date range." It's about what index design actually lets SQL Server answer that efficiently, versus falling back to scanning and aggregating the whole table.

**Why this happens in real databases.** Date-ranged aggregate reports are everywhere in real applications — sales this month, active users this week, signups this quarter — precisely because "how are we doing recently" is one of the most common questions any business asks of its own data. Without the right index, though, none of these questions can be answered by touching only the relevant recent slice of data; SQL Server ends up reading the entire history of the table just to compute a total over a tiny, recent fraction of it, and that gap gets worse every single day as more historical data accumulates while the "recent" slice being queried stays roughly the same size.

**How it happens mechanically inside SQL Server.** Without a helpful index, satisfying `WHERE OrderDate >= X AND OrderDate < Y` combined with a `GROUP BY`/aggregate typically means: scan the whole table (or a full nonclustered index on some other column, if one happens to exist but doesn't help with the date range), throw away every row that falls outside the date range, and hash-aggregate whatever's left. The cost of that full scan is tied to the *entire* table's size, not to how many rows actually fall in the requested range — so as historical data piles up month after month, this query gets slower and slower even though the actual amount of relevant data being summarized stays roughly constant.

A well-designed covering index changes this in two ways at once. First, if the index's leading column is the date column being filtered, SQL Server can seek directly to the start of the requested range and then simply walk forward through the index only as far as the range extends, reading a number of index pages roughly proportional to the *size of the range*, not the size of the whole table — a small, recent slice stays cheap to read no matter how much old history has piled up behind it. Second, if the index also "covers" the query — meaning it includes, via `INCLUDE`, whatever columns are actually being summed or counted — SQL Server never needs to go back to the full table row to fetch those values; everything needed for the aggregation is already sitting right there in the index it's already walking. Combined, this turns "scan everything, filter out most of it, then aggregate" into "seek to the start of the range, walk only the matching slice, aggregate as you go, using data already present in the index" — the aggregate operator even gets to work incrementally as it walks the already-relevant, already-present data, often as a cheap Stream Aggregate rather than a Hash Aggregate, similar to the indexed `GROUP BY` case elsewhere in this course.

**Why this matters in production.** This exact query shape — "totals for the current period, filtered by date, out of a table that keeps growing" — is one of the most common report and dashboard queries in real business software, and it's also one of the most likely to quietly get slower and slower over time purely because the underlying table keeps accumulating history, even while the application code and the query itself never change. Because the degradation is gradual, it often isn't noticed until a report that used to run in a second is suddenly taking many seconds, months or years after it was first built. The fix demonstrated in this lesson — a covering index with the date column leading, including whatever's being aggregated — decouples the query's cost from the table's total historical size entirely, tying it instead to the size of the requested range, so the query stays fast indefinitely regardless of how much history piles up behind it.

**Try it yourself.** The scenario below aggregates a recent date range out of a much larger historical table with no supporting index, and shows you a full scan reading the entire table's history just to total up a small recent slice. After adding a covering index leading with the date column, re-run the same query and watch the plan seek directly to the start of the range and stop reading the moment it passes the end — with logical reads that scale with the size of the requested range, not with however much history has piled up in the table over time.

**Beyond this exact scenario.** This same range-plus-aggregate pattern extends naturally to rolling windows — "last 7 days," "trailing 90 days," "year to date" — which are even more common in real dashboards than a fixed calendar-month range, and benefit from the exact same covering, date-leading index design. It's also worth watching for this pattern specifically on any table that never purges old data: a table that only ever grows, combined with a report that only ever looks at a recent slice, is the textbook setup for this exact kind of "worked fine at launch, slowly got worse over years" degradation.

One more detail worth knowing: if the aggregate also groups by a second column (say, region as well as date), the composite index should generally lead with whichever column is used in the range filter, then include the group-by column next, so the index still supports seeking into the date range efficiently while also keeping same-group rows together for the aggregate step.

## Scenario
A sales report groups recent orders by status:

```sql
SELECT Status, COUNT(*), SUM(Total)
FROM Orders
WHERE OrderDate >= '2025-11-01'
GROUP BY Status;
```

The recent window is a small fraction of the table, yet the query reads **all 200,000 rows** every run.

## Why it's slow
The only index is the clustered PK on `OrderId`. Nothing supports the `OrderDate` filter, so SQL Server does a **Clustered Index Scan** of the whole table, then a **Hash Aggregate** — even though only ~16,000 rows fall in the window.

## The concept
An index on the **filter column** `OrderDate` lets SQL **seek** straight to the recent slice. Add the columns the aggregate needs (`Status`, `Total`) as **INCLUDE**d columns so the index is **covering** — no lookups back to the table. The engine then reads only the slice, not the whole table.

## What to look for
- Before: **Clustered Index Scan** + **Hash Match** over ~all rows (hundreds+ logical reads).
- After: an **Index Seek** over just the window; logical reads drop by an order of magnitude.

The fix: `CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX ... ON Orders(OrderDate) INCLUDE (Status, Total);`
startingQuery:
SELECT Status, COUNT(*) AS Cnt, SUM(Total) AS Revenue
FROM Orders
WHERE OrderDate >= '2025-11-01'
GROUP BY Status;
hints: The filter is on OrderDate but nothing indexes it — the plan scans the whole table before aggregating.
Index the filter column so SQL can seek the recent slice, and INCLUDE the aggregate's columns (Status, Total) so it never leaves the index.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_OrderDate_Cov ON Orders(OrderDate) INCLUDE (Status, Total);
